assumptions: Nationwide administrative practice permits economically attractive projects without prohibitive friction.
At least one customer class will fund independent coordination rather than procure a bundled incumbent solution.
Specialists can be hired within the stated capital while the founder retains control of customer economics.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Five paid feasibility studies yielding at least one signed multi-year coordination mandate with verified savings, meter-data access, clear counterparty responsibilities, and fully loaded contribution economics.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Expanded virtual-prosumer rules create a genuine coordination gap across generation, participants, allocation, contracts, meter data, and settlement.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Professional coordination costs exist, but achievable savings, project conversion, payer authority, and actual budgets remain immature and unverified.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Large projects and recurring settlement could be valuable, but 150-500 delivery hours, specialist costs, long payback, procurement, and uncertain conversion weaken economics.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Portfolio feasibility studies offer a bounded entry, but the eligible, economical project pool after nationwide implementation is unknown.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: The proposed mandate could be valuable, yet no project, contract, data right, or exclusive channel is held and large energy incumbents are advantaged.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: Successful projects could extend into recurring settlement, energy optimization, financing, participant administration, and broader portfolio coordination.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Multi-year mandates and implementation playbooks can create switching costs, but they depend on many counterparties and are presently unsigned.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Independent allocation modeling may improve decisions, though energy sellers, ESCOs, and developers can bundle legal, metering, and operational execution.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Nationwide expansion in October 2026 is a strong immediate catalyst, albeit one with immature operating practice.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Installer and property-adviser referrals are conceivable, but municipal and property sales are slow and no repeatable acquisition path is validated.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Energy law, metering, procurement, multi-party contracting, and intensive project management exceed what AI alone solves and poorly fit a part-time low-social-load launch.

highest_value_structural_change: Partner with an energy seller or property platform to obtain standardized data access and repeatable multi-project mandates instead of assembling each project independently.
main_structural_strength: A successful coordination mandate can become recurring and sticky because it sits across allocation, data, contracts, and monthly settlement.
primary_score_limiter: The model depends on unsigned multi-party rights, uncertain post-launch economics, and specialist-heavy execution that conflicts with founder constraints.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Nationwide operation is only beginning, while energy-law and metering complexity favor established retailers, ESCOs, and developers with existing counterparties.
